Quick overview: Proposition 1
LAist's AirTalk host Larry Mantle's ballot cram session gets you ready to vote with guests Michael Alvarez, of Caltech, Sara Sadhwani of Pomona College, and Lee E. Ohanian of UCLA and the Hoover Institution.
This measure asks voters to approve $11.25 billion in state bonds for various affordable housing strategies. The revenue would go toward the construction of new income-restricted apartments, supportive housing for tenants overcoming homelessness, mortgage assistance for veterans and a number of other programs.
What’s at stake?
According to recent U.S. Census Bureau statistics (https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48945), about 54% of California renters officially qualify as “cost-burdened,” meaning they pay more than 30% of their income on rent. The only states with higher levels of rent burden are Florida and Nevada.
California needs to build about 1 million new homes (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/affordable-housing-units-setback-california) specifically for low-income residents, based on current statewide planning goals. Proposition 1 aims to speed up that process by raising money from bonds that would be repaid from the state’s general fund over the next 25 years.
Official title on the ballot: Prop. 1: Authorizes bonds for housing affordability programs
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/index.htm) on the ballot:
Authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable housing, and downpayment assistance. Fiscal Impact : Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the housing bond.
What your vote means
A "yes" vote means: The state could borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
A "no" vote means: The state could not borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
Understanding Prop. 1
Affordable housing units generally set rents at no more than 30% of a tenant’s income. That means they often do not generate enough rental income to be profitable for developers. That’s where public subsidies come in.
In recent years, California has put more funding toward creating low-cost housing. According to a recent state legislative analysis (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billAnalysisClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), California has funded various affordable housing programs with $8 billion from the state’s general fund since 2019.
But some of those funding streams are now drying up.
A previous measure also called Proposition 1, passed by voters in 2018, approved $4 billion in bonds for affordable housing and veteran mortgage programs. Proposition 2, also from 2018, put $2 billion toward the creation of 7,000 supportive units for formerly unhoused tenants. Both funds are now depleted.
Those state funds have run out at a time when state lawmakers say California can no longer rely on Washington, D.C., to expand or continue federal affordable housing efforts. They argue Prop. 1 could make an immediate difference for an estimated 45,000 units that are in the construction pipeline but have yet to break ground due to a lack of gap financing.
Here’s what supporters say
In addition to helping low-income renters, formerly unhoused tenants and veterans, Proposition 1 proponents say the bond would also fund programs specifically designed to help college students, youth exiting foster care, farmworkers, tribal communities and low-income first-time homebuyers.
Notable endorsements: The coalition (https://yesonprop1ca.com/coalition) of Proposition 1 supporters includes the Southern California Association of Nonprofit Housing, the California Association of Veterans Service Agencies and the California Federation of Labor Unions.
Here’s what opponents say
There is no organized campaign against Proposition 1, but a handful of Republican state lawmakers voted against putting it on the ballot. State Sen. Tony Strickland, who represents coastal Orange County and pockets of L.A. County, said Proposition 1 has a “noble goal” but could end up “bankrupting our next generation.” He said, “We could definitely find $10 billion within the general fund spending, and within our normal budget, without doing bond indebtedness.”
Notable opposition: The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a frequent critic of new California revenue proposals, opposes Proposition 1 in its election guide (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/). The group writes that bonds rely on borrowed money, and debt service costs add up over time. "When used to pay for programs instead of capital projects, it’s a much greater burden on taxpayers than just paying for these programs from the budget," the Howard Jarvis guide says.
Potential financial impact
The California Legislative Analyst’s Office said (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026) repayment of the Proposition 1 bonds would cost the state between $500 million and $600 million each year for the next 25 years.
Because bonds would need to be repaid with interest, the legislative analysis said costs would likely end up about 15% higher than if the state paid for the programs with existing funding.
In total, the analysis said Proposition 1 would provide subsidies for an estimated 40,000 rental apartments, 2,500 farmworker units, 1,200 college student beds and would help up to 40,000 households achieve homeownership, including about 2,100 veterans.

Quick overview: Proposition 1
LAist's AirTalk host Larry Mantle's ballot cram session gets you ready to vote with guests Michael Alvarez, of Caltech, Sara Sadhwani of Pomona College, and Lee E. Ohanian of UCLA and the Hoover Institution.
This measure asks voters to approve $11.25 billion in state bonds for various affordable housing strategies. The revenue would go toward the construction of new income-restricted apartments, supportive housing for tenants overcoming homelessness, mortgage assistance for veterans and a number of other programs.
What’s at stake?
According to recent U.S. Census Bureau statistics (https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48945), about 54% of California renters officially qualify as “cost-burdened,” meaning they pay more than 30% of their income on rent. The only states with higher levels of rent burden are Florida and Nevada.
California needs to build about 1 million new homes (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/affordable-housing-units-setback-california) specifically for low-income residents, based on current statewide planning goals. Proposition 1 aims to speed up that process by raising money from bonds that would be repaid from the state’s general fund over the next 25 years.
Official title on the ballot: Prop. 1: Authorizes bonds for housing affordability programs
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/index.htm) on the ballot:
Authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable housing, and downpayment assistance. Fiscal Impact : Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the housing bond.
What your vote means
A "yes" vote means: The state could borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
A "no" vote means: The state could not borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
Understanding Prop. 1
Affordable housing units generally set rents at no more than 30% of a tenant’s income. That means they often do not generate enough rental income to be profitable for developers. That’s where public subsidies come in.
In recent years, California has put more funding toward creating low-cost housing. According to a recent state legislative analysis (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billAnalysisClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), California has funded various affordable housing programs with $8 billion from the state’s general fund since 2019.
But some of those funding streams are now drying up.
A previous measure also called Proposition 1, passed by voters in 2018, approved $4 billion in bonds for affordable housing and veteran mortgage programs. Proposition 2, also from 2018, put $2 billion toward the creation of 7,000 supportive units for formerly unhoused tenants. Both funds are now depleted.
Those state funds have run out at a time when state lawmakers say California can no longer rely on Washington, D.C., to expand or continue federal affordable housing efforts. They argue Prop. 1 could make an immediate difference for an estimated 45,000 units that are in the construction pipeline but have yet to break ground due to a lack of gap financing.
Here’s what supporters say
In addition to helping low-income renters, formerly unhoused tenants and veterans, Proposition 1 proponents say the bond would also fund programs specifically designed to help college students, youth exiting foster care, farmworkers, tribal communities and low-income first-time homebuyers.
Notable endorsements: The coalition (https://yesonprop1ca.com/coalition) of Proposition 1 supporters includes the Southern California Association of Nonprofit Housing, the California Association of Veterans Service Agencies and the California Federation of Labor Unions.
Here’s what opponents say
There is no organized campaign against Proposition 1, but a handful of Republican state lawmakers voted against putting it on the ballot. State Sen. Tony Strickland, who represents coastal Orange County and pockets of L.A. County, said Proposition 1 has a “noble goal” but could end up “bankrupting our next generation.” He said, “We could definitely find $10 billion within the general fund spending, and within our normal budget, without doing bond indebtedness.”
Notable opposition: The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a frequent critic of new California revenue proposals, opposes Proposition 1 in its election guide (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/). The group writes that bonds rely on borrowed money, and debt service costs add up over time. "When used to pay for programs instead of capital projects, it’s a much greater burden on taxpayers than just paying for these programs from the budget," the Howard Jarvis guide says.
Potential financial impact
The California Legislative Analyst’s Office said (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026) repayment of the Proposition 1 bonds would cost the state between $500 million and $600 million each year for the next 25 years.
Because bonds would need to be repaid with interest, the legislative analysis said costs would likely end up about 15% higher than if the state paid for the programs with existing funding.
In total, the analysis said Proposition 1 would provide subsidies for an estimated 40,000 rental apartments, 2,500 farmworker units, 1,200 college student beds and would help up to 40,000 households achieve homeownership, including about 2,100 veterans.

content.thinking:
Interesting context: cost per unit ~$630-660k. $10B for 40,000 units = $250k subsidy per unit (partial subsidy). That's consistent with the stacking approach.

Now, let me consider the substantive policy question: Is it "better" to vote yes or no? This is a judgment call. Let me weigh:

Arguments for YES:
1. California has an extreme housing affordability crisis: 2.5M home shortfall; ~180,000 homeless; nearly half of renters cost-burdened.
2. Subsidized affordable housing cannot be built without public subsidy; the state's programs are oversubscribed 9:1, and 40,000-46,000 units are permitted, designed, and partially funded but stalled awaiting the last bit of state money. This bond would unlock those units, leveraging ~$4 from other sources per $1 state dollar.
3. GO bonds are appropriate for long-lived capital assets with 55-year affordability covenants — asset life exceeds debt life. (Contrast with Prop 38 research bond.)
4. Debt-service burden is modest in context: ~$550M/yr = 0.25% of GF budget; state debt service ~3% of GF revenue vs 4% historical average, meaning there is below-average capacity.
5. The veterans' portion ($1.25B) is self-financing at no cost to taxpayers.
6. Broad, diverse support: veterans groups, teachers, mayors, cities/counties, labor, Habitat for Humanity, UC/CSU, CA Democratic Party, most major editorial boards (SF Chronicle, McClatchy/Sac Bee, Daily Californian, Daily Bruin), and 60% of likely voters. No formal opposition campaign; no argument against submitted for the official guide.
7. Recent state streamlining reforms (2025-2026 housing overhaul, CEQA reform, impact fee reductions, new Housing and Homelessness Agency/HDFC one-stop shop) reduce cost per unit and improve delivery efficiency, meaning bond dollars go further than in past cycles. This addresses the classic "money alone won't fix it" critique: regulation has been reformed, and the binding constraint now is capital.
8. Federal funding cuts (LIHTC/HOME pressure, federal retrenchment) make state capital more important.

Arguments for NO:
1. State has structural deficits ($14-18B in 2026-27; $10B+/yr ongoing per DOF; LAO projected $35B/yr by 2027-28 before revenue upgrades). Adding $550M/yr of debt service for 25-30 years reduces budget flexibility at a time when deficits force cuts.
2. Already $80B outstanding debt, $40B authorized but unsold, ~$6B/yr debt service. Total cost $17.4B for $10B borrowed.
3. Earmarked, prescriptive allocations across many constituencies (student housing, tribes, farmworkers, pilots) rather than prioritized to highest-impact use; "veterans" in the title but only ~11% to veterans (and that part is self-financing).
4. Core problem may be production costs/regulation rather than lack of subsidy; pouring money into an inefficient system inflates prices and subsidizes high-cost developers (per-unit costs ~$660k, twice peer states). Some argue the state should fund from the budget rather than debt (HJTA).
5. Alternative uses of scarce borrowing capacity (e.g., Prop 38 competes for the same capacity; or debt payoff — Prop 2 would let reserves pay down debt, including $20B owed to federal government).

Weighing: How significant is $550M/year against a ~$230-250B General Fund? ~0.25%. That's small. The state's debt ratio is below historical average. The purpose is capital infrastructure with a 55-year life — exactly the textbook use of GO debt. Meanwhile the need is acute and the pipeline of shovel-ready units is real (40,000+ units stalled for want of the last tranche of subsidy). Leverage of 4:1 means $10B could unlock $40-50B of total investment.

The counterargument about structural deficits is real, but $550M/yr is ~3% of an $18B deficit — it wouldn't be the difference between balance and imbalance, and the deficit exists regardless. Also, deferring capital investment doesn't fix the structural deficit; and housing costs impose huge ongoing state/local costs (homelessness services, Medi-Cal, etc.). Supportive housing saves $1.80 per $1 invested in public costs.

The efficiency critique is legitimate, but 2025-26 reforms (impact fee cuts, streamlining, HDFC consolidation, $60-70k/unit cost reductions) target exactly that, and the measure includes $200M for local pilot programs aimed at building at lower cost.

Also note: this is a legislatively referred bond, passed with bipartisan majorities exceeding two-thirds, and no organized opposition, no argument against in the official guide, no opposition funds. That's a signal of broad consensus.

Given the modest relative fiscal cost, the acute need, appropriate use of long-term debt for a 55-year asset, high leverage of stalled projects, and the absence of any organized opposition, the balance favors YES.

Let me do a bit more verification on a couple of items to be thorough:
- Check that Prop 2 (rainy day fund) doesn't interact problematically. Not needed.
- Check LAist's guide for balanced treatment; check the "californiachoices.org" con; and maybe check the Mercury News / East Bay Times endorsement (I recall McClatchy = yes). Also check whether there's criticism about the measure's accountability provisions (audits). And confirm campaign finance: $12M+ raised by Yes; Airbnb $1M, Brin PAC $1M, carpenters unions $2M. Some might criticize developer/union self-interest, but it's a housing bond — expected.

Let me also double check whether there are any concerns about "no new taxes" claim and whether General Fund backstop for CalVet. Also check any watchdog analysis of prior housing bonds' performance (2018 Prop 1: $4B — did it deliver? Units produced?). That's relevant evidence for effectiveness. Let me search for the 2018 Prop 1 housing bond outcomes.

Quick overview: Proposition 1
LAist's AirTalk host Larry Mantle's ballot cram session gets you ready to vote with guests Michael Alvarez, of Caltech, Sara Sadhwani of Pomona College, and Lee E. Ohanian of UCLA and the Hoover Institution.
This measure asks voters to approve $11.25 billion in state bonds for various affordable housing strategies. The revenue would go toward the construction of new income-restricted apartments, supportive housing for tenants overcoming homelessness, mortgage assistance for veterans and a number of other programs.
What’s at stake?
According to recent U.S. Census Bureau statistics (https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48945), about 54% of California renters officially qualify as “cost-burdened,” meaning they pay more than 30% of their income on rent. The only states with higher levels of rent burden are Florida and Nevada.
California needs to build about 1 million new homes (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/affordable-housing-units-setback-california) specifically for low-income residents, based on current statewide planning goals. Proposition 1 aims to speed up that process by raising money from bonds that would be repaid from the state’s general fund over the next 25 years.
Official title on the ballot: Prop. 1: Authorizes bonds for housing affordability programs
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/index.htm) on the ballot:
Authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable housing, and downpayment assistance. Fiscal Impact : Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the housing bond.
What your vote means
A "yes" vote means: The state could borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
A "no" vote means: The state could not borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
Understanding Prop. 1
Affordable housing units generally set rents at no more than 30% of a tenant’s income. That means they often do not generate enough rental income to be profitable for developers. That’s where public subsidies come in.
In recent years, California has put more funding toward creating low-cost housing. According to a recent state legislative analysis (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billAnalysisClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), California has funded various affordable housing programs with $8 billion from the state’s general fund since 2019.
But some of those funding streams are now drying up.
A previous measure also called Proposition 1, passed by voters in 2018, approved $4 billion in bonds for affordable housing and veteran mortgage programs. Proposition 2, also from 2018, put $2 billion toward the creation of 7,000 supportive units for formerly unhoused tenants. Both funds are now depleted.
Those state funds have run out at a time when state lawmakers say California can no longer rely on Washington, D.C., to expand or continue federal affordable housing efforts. They argue Prop. 1 could make an immediate difference for an estimated 45,000 units that are in the construction pipeline but have yet to break ground due to a lack of gap financing.
Here’s what supporters say
In addition to helping low-income renters, formerly unhoused tenants and veterans, Proposition 1 proponents say the bond would also fund programs specifically designed to help college students, youth exiting foster care, farmworkers, tribal communities and low-income first-time homebuyers.
Notable endorsements: The coalition (https://yesonprop1ca.com/coalition) of Proposition 1 supporters includes the Southern California Association of Nonprofit Housing, the California Association of Veterans Service Agencies and the California Federation of Labor Unions.
Here’s what opponents say
There is no organized campaign against Proposition 1, but a handful of Republican state lawmakers voted against putting it on the ballot. State Sen. Tony Strickland, who represents coastal Orange County and pockets of L.A. County, said Proposition 1 has a “noble goal” but could end up “bankrupting our next generation.” He said, “We could definitely find $10 billion within the general fund spending, and within our normal budget, without doing bond indebtedness.”
Notable opposition: The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a frequent critic of new California revenue proposals, opposes Proposition 1 in its election guide (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/). The group writes that bonds rely on borrowed money, and debt service costs add up over time. "When used to pay for programs instead of capital projects, it’s a much greater burden on taxpayers than just paying for these programs from the budget," the Howard Jarvis guide says.
Potential financial impact
The California Legislative Analyst’s Office said (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026) repayment of the Proposition 1 bonds would cost the state between $500 million and $600 million each year for the next 25 years.
Because bonds would need to be repaid with interest, the legislative analysis said costs would likely end up about 15% higher than if the state paid for the programs with existing funding.
In total, the analysis said Proposition 1 would provide subsidies for an estimated 40,000 rental apartments, 2,500 farmworker units, 1,200 college student beds and would help up to 40,000 households achieve homeownership, including about 2,100 veterans.

A majority is needed to pass.

Very useful. Key evidence on effectiveness of the 2018 bond: $4 billion bond (of which $3B general housing) produced 22,735 units by FY2023-24 — roughly $132k of bond money per unit produced (or ~$176k per unit for the $3B portion). This new $10B bond targets up to 40,000 units = $250k per unit (LAO estimate for subsidies, which is per-unit subsidy not per-unit total cost). Hmm, actually the 2018 bond's $3B produced 22,735 units = $132k/unit of bond subsidy. This bond's $10B for ~40,000 units + 40,000 homeownership households = less leverage per unit? Let's see: LAO says the bond funds would provide subsidies for up to 40,000 multifamily rental units. $7.2B multifamily / 40,000 = $180k per unit subsidy. Plus homeownership assistance for 40,000 households with $1.1B = $27.5k per household. That's reasonable.

Also, SPUR voter guide — let me check SPUR's recommendation on Prop 1 (SPUR is a Bay Area planning org; they usually endorse yes). Also let me check the "californiachoices.org" con and maybe Lee Ohanian's view (he's a UCLA economist, generally skeptical). Let me also check the CalTax (California Taxpayers Association) position — one source said CalTax and HJTA oppose; another said they back it (that was about a different prop — Prop 5 or 43, the "Legislature placed it on the ballot in a June deal with HJTA which withdrew its own broader local-tax initiative" — that referred to Prop 43). So CalTax/HJTA oppose Prop 1.

Let me look at a couple more sources: SPUR's guide and any analysis from the Reason Foundation / CalPolicy or an economist view on whether housing bonds are good value. Also check the Mercury News/OC Register "no" editorial reasoning, and the LA Times editorial board position (Skelton said no; the LA Times editorial board — cityhallpass said no LA Times editorial board position as of Sept 30; the last-minute guide may have included an editorial board view). Let me check the LA Times last-minute guide section on Prop 1 for the editorial board's stance.

Actually, I have enough. But let me consider deeper policy economics: Does subsidizing affordable housing help overall affordability? Economists generally agree that building more housing of any kind helps affordability, and subsidies are needed for the lowest income segments since LIHTC alone doesn't cover ELI housing. However, some economists (e.g., Lee Ohanian) argue that California should deregulate rather than subsidize, and that subsidies mostly raise construction costs.

Counter: California has done significant deregulation (SB 330, AB 2011, SB 6, SB 4, CEQA reform 2025, impact fee reform, density bonuses). The market-rate pipeline still underperforms, and for very low-income households, subsidy is mathematically necessary (rents at 30% of income can't cover debt service at CA construction costs).

Fiscal capacity: debt service at 3% of GF revenue vs 4% historical average; new bond adds ~0.25-0.3% of GF. Even under structural deficits, $550M/yr is small relative to $18B problems, and the state has ~$40B in authorized-but-unsold bonds anyway (meaning the trajectory of debt service is already rising).

One more consideration: Opportunity cost of bonding capacity — but the state has capacity below historical averages.

Let me also weigh: is it better to vote yes given the alternative that the housing programs get no funding at all (state general fund housing investment has "largely disappeared")? Under a NO vote, the 40,000+ stalled units stay stalled and programs remain dry. That's a concrete harm. Under YES, the state takes on $550M/yr in debt service — a modest, spread cost for a 55-year asset.

Also, one risk: Prop 1 combined with Prop 38 adds $1.1B/yr; and Prop 37 is self-repaying. So the aggregate burden is still ~0.5% of GF revenue.

Also there's a nuance: the "no new taxes" claim — debt service is paid from existing revenues, so no new taxes, but it crowds out other spending. Under deficits, that crowd-out matters. But the crowd-out is small (0.25%).

Let me quickly check SPUR's recommendation and one more critical analysis (maybe Reason Foundation or a Hoover/LAO economist take), then decide.

CA
Prop
1
|
Bond
Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs
Authorizes $10 billion in general obligation bonds to fund production of affordable and supportive housing and $1.25 billion in mortgage revenue bonds to fund a homeownership program for veterans and military families.
SPUR's Recommendation
California’s housing affordability crisis continues to worsen, largely because of a supply shortage and inadequate funding to build more. Even with lower construction costs, affordable housing construction and preservation would still require significant, consistent government subsidies. Thousands of approved affordable housing projects have stalled because of a lack of financing.
General obligation bonds are needed periodically to replenish funding for the state’s main affordable housing finance programs. Prop. 1’s proposed bond funds pair with state and federal Low Income Housing Tax Credits to finance affordable housing developments. This measure is critical to expanding affordable housing opportunities for lower-income residents across California through new construction, preservation, and homebuyer assistance. Funds would be distributed through well-established state programs with a proven track record of success.
Vote YES
What Prop. 1 Would Do
According to the California Housing Partnership, Proposition 1 will help finance more than 40,000 shovel-ready affordable rental homes and help 20,000 California households attain homeownership. 1 The bond proceeds would replenish key long-standing state affordable housing financing programs and be allocated as follows:
$5.10 billion for the Multifamily Housing Program. At least 10% of units in each development receiving these funds must be affordable to extremely low-income households.
$1.25 billion in self-supporting revenue bonds for the CalVet Home Loan Program to help veterans and military families buy a home. These bonds are repaid entirely through mortgage payments and do not rely on taxpayer funding.
$1.15 billion for supportive housing administered through the Multifamily Housing Program. The program requires funding to create a reserve account to cover operating deficits for developments receiving funding.
$750 million for the Portfolio Reinvestment Program to rehabilitate and extend the long-term affordability of state-funded multifamily rental housing projects that are at risk of conversion to market-rate housing.
$600 million for the CalHOME Program for new construction of affordable ownership homes.
$500 million for the My Home down payment assistance program for lower- and moderate-income households.
$500 million for the Infill Infrastructure Grant Program of 2019 for grants supporting infrastructure needed to support developing affordable and mixed-income housing in infill locations.
$450 million to the Joe Serna, Jr. Farmworker Housing Program to fund grants or loans for the construction or rehabilitation of housing for agricultural employees and their families.
$350 million for new affordable student housing projects split evenly between the University of California and California State University systems.
$200 million for the Tribal Housing Grant Program to finance housing and housing-related activities enabling tribes to rebuild and reconstitute their communities.
$200 million for a program to be created by the Legislature that funds acquisition and rehabilitation of unrestricted housing units (i.e., unsubsidized housing that may naturally be affordable) and the attachment of long-term affordability restrictions to the units.
$200 million to the Local Housing Trust Fund Program to fund competitive grants and loans to local housing trust funds that develop, own, lend, or create or preserve affordable housing.
The Backstory
The state has historically used voter-approved general obligation bonds to fund affordable housing programs. In 2018, voters approved Proposition 1, the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2018, which provided $4 billion in funding, including $1 billion for the Department of Veterans Affairs program and $3 billion for various affordable housing programs. As of fiscal year 2023–24, when the 2018 Prop. 1 bond funding ran out, 22,735 units of housing had been produced.
Enterprise Community Partners’ 2026 California Affordable Housing Production Pipeline report, released in March, found that nearly 40,000 approved affordable housing units are frozen due to a lack of funding and could be built with this new financing source. 2
The proposed bond has undergone a rigorous process and has broad support. Over the past four years, the Legislature has introduced various affordable housing bond measures, including bills by Assemblymember Wicks and Senator Cabaldon. Those bills have moved through the legislative process over the past year and a half, giving the members of the Legislature multiple opportunities to negotiate the terms. Governor Newsom, Senate President Pro Tem Limón, and Assembly Speaker Rivas negotiated final amendments for the authorizing legislation, SB 417, the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026. The State Legislature voted with supermajorities in each house to place the proposition on the November 2026 ballot.
Legislative analyses of the measure find the total cost to pay off the bonds would be approximately $17.39 billion in principal and interest. Average annual debt service payments from the State’s General Fund are estimated at approximately $580 million when all bonds are sold, assuming an interest rate of 4.02% and a 30-year maturity. This amount of annual debt service represents about 0.26% of the State’s General Fund budget.
According to the State of California Debt Affordability Report issued by the state treasurer in October 2025, California’s ratio of General Fund-supported debt service to General Fund revenues was 3.59% in fiscal year 2024–25 and was estimated to be 3.95% in fiscal year 2025–26 . 3 This ratio is in line with the 4% historical average for bonded indebtedness.
A simple majority (50% plus one vote) of California voters is required to pass Prop. 1.
Equity Impacts
The Bay Area Equity Atlas finds that all nine Bay Area counties struggle to come anywhere close to meeting their state-mandated share of new housing construction. In 2023 and 2024, the Bay Area permitted just 9% of its required units, including only 5% of required very-low-income units and 10% of required low-income units. 4
This lack of affordable housing options increases displacement pressures on lower-income households and households of color. The Bay Area Equity Atlas’s Black Communities and the Bay Area's Housing Crisis report, published in April 2025, found the Bay Area lost more than 5,000 Black-owned households during the 2010s, with significant declines in historic Black communities in the East Bay, San Francisco, and Solano County, while the number of Black renter households increased by just 300. 5
Sufficient funding to create below-market-rate rental and homeownership opportunities will help address the affordability challenges and displacement pressures faced by lower-income households, Black households, and other households of color.
Pros
The state faces a chronic affordable housing crisis that cannot be addressed without significant ongoing public investment to lower housing costs for lower-income households.
The bond would make the most of recent federal changes to the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit program that allow California to nearly double its affordable housing production: if the state invests $4.1 billion annually, it can leverage $6.7 billion in available federal funding.
The funding would be distributed through existing state programs with a proven track record of producing affordable housing options for lower-income residents.
The Bay Area is well positioned to use the funds effectively, given the number of highly effective nonprofit affordable housing developers here.
Con
The bond would contribute to the state’s debt burden, with debt service on the bond representing 0.26% of the overall State General Fund budget.

Authorizes $10 billion in general obligation bonds to fund production of affordable and supportive housing and $1.25 billion in mortgage revenue bonds to fund a homeownership program for veterans and military families.
SPUR's Recommendation
California’s housing affordability crisis continues to worsen, largely because of a supply shortage and inadequate funding to build more. Even with lower construction costs, affordable housing construction and preservation would still require significant, consistent government subsidies. Thousands of approved affordable housing projects have stalled because of a lack of financing.
General obligation bonds are needed periodically to replenish funding for the state’s main affordable housing finance programs. Prop. 1’s proposed bond funds pair with state and federal Low Income Housing Tax Credits to finance affordable housing developments. This measure is critical to expanding affordable housing opportunities for lower-income residents across California through new construction, preservation, and homebuyer assistance. Funds would be distributed through well-established state programs with a proven track record of success.

According to the California Housing Partnership, Proposition 1 will help finance more than 40,000 shovel-ready affordable rental homes and help 20,000 California households attain homeownership. 1 The bond proceeds would replenish key long-standing state affordable housing financing programs and be allocated as follows:

$1.25 billion in self-supporting revenue bonds for the CalVet Home Loan Program to help veterans and military families buy a home. These bonds are repaid entirely through mortgage payments and do not rely on taxpayer funding.

$750 million for the Portfolio Reinvestment Program to rehabilitate and extend the long-term affordability of state-funded multifamily rental housing projects that are at risk of conversion to market-rate housing.
$600 million for the CalHOME Program for new construction of affordable ownership homes.
$500 million for the My Home down payment assistance program for lower- and moderate-income households.
$500 million for the Infill Infrastructure Grant Program of 2019 for grants supporting infrastructure needed to support developing affordable and mixed-income housing in infill locations.
$450 million to the Joe Serna, Jr. Farmworker Housing Program to fund grants or loans for the construction or rehabilitation of housing for agricultural employees and their families.

Average annual debt service payments from the State’s General Fund are estimated at approximately $580 million when all bonds are sold, assuming an interest rate of 4.02% and a 30-year maturity. This amount of annual debt service represents about 0.26% of the State’s General Fund budget.

Prop
1

Bond
Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs
Authorizes $10 billion in general obligation bonds to fund production of affordable and supportive housing and $1.25 billion in mortgage revenue bonds to fund a homeownership program for veterans and military families.
SPUR's Recommendation
California’s housing affordability crisis continues to worsen, largely because of a supply shortage and inadequate funding to build more. Even with lower construction costs, affordable housing construction and preservation would still require significant, consistent government subsidies. Thousands of approved affordable housing projects have stalled because of a lack of financing.
General obligation bonds are needed periodically to replenish funding for the state’s main affordable housing finance programs. Prop. 1’s proposed bond funds pair with state and federal Low Income Housing Tax Credits to finance affordable housing developments. This measure is critical to expanding affordable housing opportunities for lower-income residents across California through new construction, preservation, and homebuyer assistance. Funds would be distributed through well-established state programs with a proven track record of success.
Vote YES
What Prop. 1 Would Do
According to the California Housing Partnership, Proposition 1 will help finance more than 40,000 shovel-ready affordable rental homes and help 20,000 California households attain homeownership. 1 The bond proceeds would replenish key long-standing state affordable housing financing programs and be allocated as follows:
$5.10 billion for the Multifamily Housing Program. At least 10% of units in each development receiving these funds must be affordable to extremely low-income households.
$1.25 billion in self-supporting revenue bonds for the CalVet Home Loan Program to help veterans and military families buy a home. These bonds are repaid entirely through mortgage payments and do not rely on taxpayer funding.
$1.15 billion for supportive housing administered through the Multifamily Housing Program. The program requires funding to create a reserve account to cover operating deficits for developments receiving funding.
$750 million for the Portfolio Reinvestment Program to rehabilitate and extend the long-term affordability of state-funded multifamily rental housing projects that are at risk of conversion to market-rate housing.
$600 million for the CalHOME Program for new construction of affordable ownership homes.
$500 million for the My Home down payment assistance program for lower- and moderate-income households.
$500 million for the Infill Infrastructure Grant Program of 2019 for grants supporting infrastructure needed to support developing affordable and mixed-income housing in infill locations.
$450 million to the Joe Serna, Jr. Farmworker Housing Program to fund grants or loans for the construction or rehabilitation of housing for agricultural employees and their families.
$350 million for new affordable student housing projects split evenly between the University of California and California State University systems.
$200 million for the Tribal Housing Grant Program to finance housing and housing-related activities enabling tribes to rebuild and reconstitute their communities.
$200 million for a program to be created by the Legislature that funds acquisition and rehabilitation of unrestricted housing units (i.e., unsubsidized housing that may naturally be affordable) and the attachment of long-term affordability restrictions to the units.
$200 million to the Local Housing Trust Fund Program to fund competitive grants and loans to local housing trust funds that develop, own, lend, or create or preserve affordable housing.
The Backstory
The state has historically used voter-approved general obligation bonds to fund affordable housing programs. In 2018, voters approved Proposition 1, the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2018, which provided $4 billion in funding, including $1 billion for the Department of Veterans Affairs program and $3 billion for various affordable housing programs. As of fiscal year 2023–24, when the 2018 Prop. 1 bond funding ran out, 22,735 units of housing had been produced.
Enterprise Community Partners’ 2026 California Affordable Housing Production Pipeline report, released in March, found that nearly 40,000 approved affordable housing units are frozen due to a lack of funding and could be built with this new financing source. 2
The proposed bond has undergone a rigorous process and has broad support. Over the past four years, the Legislature has introduced various affordable housing bond measures, including bills by Assemblymember Wicks and Senator Cabaldon. Those bills have moved through the legislative process over the past year and a half, giving the members of the Legislature multiple opportunities to negotiate the terms. Governor Newsom, Senate President Pro Tem Limón, and Assembly Speaker Rivas negotiated final amendments for the authorizing legislation, SB 417, the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026. The State Legislature voted with supermajorities in each house to place the proposition on the November 2026 ballot.
Legislative analyses of the measure find the total cost to pay off the bonds would be approximately $17.39 billion in principal and interest. Average annual debt service payments from the State’s General Fund are estimated at approximately $580 million when all bonds are sold, assuming an interest rate of 4.02% and a 30-year maturity. This amount of annual debt service represents about 0.26% of the State’s General Fund budget.
According to the State of California Debt Affordability Report issued by the state treasurer in October 2025, California’s ratio of General Fund-supported debt service to General Fund revenues was 3.59% in fiscal year 2024–25 and was estimated to be 3.95% in fiscal year 2025–26 . 3 This ratio is in line with the 4% historical average for bonded indebtedness.
A simple majority (50% plus one vote) of California voters is required to pass Prop. 1.
Equity Impacts
The Bay Area Equity Atlas finds that all nine Bay Area counties struggle to come anywhere close to meeting their state-mandated share of new housing construction. In 2023 and 2024, the Bay Area permitted just 9% of its required units, including only 5% of required very-low-income units and 10% of required low-income units. 4
This lack of affordable housing options increases displacement pressures on lower-income households and households of color. The Bay Area Equity Atlas’s Black Communities and the Bay Area's Housing Crisis report, published in April 2025, found the Bay Area lost more than 5,000 Black-owned households during the 2010s, with significant declines in historic Black communities in the East Bay, San Francisco, and Solano County, while the number of Black renter households increased by just 300. 5
Sufficient funding to create below-market-rate rental and homeownership opportunities will help address the affordability challenges and displacement pressures faced by lower-income households, Black households, and other households of color.
Pros
The state faces a chronic affordable housing crisis that cannot be addressed without significant ongoing public investment to lower housing costs for lower-income households.
The bond would make the most of recent federal changes to the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit program that allow California to nearly double its affordable housing production: if the state invests $4.1 billion annually, it can leverage $6.7 billion in available federal funding.
The funding would be distributed through existing state programs with a proven track record of producing affordable housing options for lower-income residents.
The Bay Area is well positioned to use the funds effectively, given the number of highly effective nonprofit affordable housing developers here.
Con
The bond would contribute to the state’s debt burden, with debt service on the bond representing 0.26% of the overall State General Fund budget.

Very useful. Key evidence on effectiveness of the 2018 bond: $4 billion bond (of which $3B general housing) produced 22,735 units by FY2023-24 — roughly $132k of bond money per unit produced (or ~$176k per unit for the $3B portion). This new $10B bond targets up to 40,000 units = $250k per unit (LAO estimate for subsidies, which is per-unit subsidy not per-unit total cost). Hmm, actually the 2018 bond's $3B produced 22,735 units = $132k/unit of bond subsidy. This bond's $10B for ~40,000 units + 40,000 homeownership households = less leverage per unit? Let's see: LAO says the bond funds would provide subsidies for up to 40,000 multifamily rental units. $7.2B multifamily / 40,000 = $180k per unit subsidy. Plus homeownership assistance for 40,000 households with $1.1B = $27.5k per household. That's reasonable.

Also, SPUR voter guide — let me check SPUR's recommendation on Prop 1 (SPUR is a Bay Area planning org; they usually endorse yes). Also let me check the "californiachoices.org" con and maybe Lee Ohanian's view (he's a UCLA economist, generally skeptical). Let me also check the CalTax (California Taxpayers Association) position — one source said CalTax and HJTA oppose; another said they back it (that was about a different prop — Prop 5 or 43, the "Legislature placed it on the ballot in a June deal with HJTA which withdrew its own broader local-tax initiative" — that referred to Prop 43). So CalTax/HJTA oppose Prop 1.

Let me look at a couple more sources: SPUR's guide and any analysis from the Reason Foundation / CalPolicy or an economist view on whether housing bonds are good value. Also check the Mercury News/OC Register "no" editorial reasoning, and the LA Times editorial board position (Skelton said no; the LA Times editorial board — cityhallpass said no LA Times editorial board position as of Sept 30; the last-minute guide may have included an editorial board view). Let me check the LA Times last-minute guide section on Prop 1 for the editorial board's stance.

Actually, I have enough. But let me consider deeper policy economics: Does subsidizing affordable housing help overall affordability? Economists generally agree that building more housing of any kind helps affordability, and subsidies are needed for the lowest income segments since LIHTC alone doesn't cover ELI housing. However, some economists (e.g., Lee Ohanian) argue that California should deregulate rather than subsidize, and that subsidies mostly raise construction costs.

Counter: California has done significant deregulation (SB 330, AB 2011, SB 6, SB 4, CEQA reform 2025, impact fee reform, density bonuses). The market-rate pipeline still underperforms, and for very low-income households, subsidy is mathematically necessary (rents at 30% of income can't cover debt service at CA construction costs).

Fiscal capacity: debt service at 3% of GF revenue vs 4% historical average; new bond adds ~0.25-0.3% of GF. Even under structural deficits, $550M/yr is small relative to $18B problems, and the state has ~$40B in authorized-but-unsold bonds anyway (meaning the trajectory of debt service is already rising).

One more consideration: Opportunity cost of bonding capacity — but the state has capacity below historical averages.

Let me also weigh: is it better to vote yes given the alternative that the housing programs get no funding at all (state general fund housing investment has "largely disappeared")? Under a NO vote, the 40,000+ stalled units stay stalled and programs remain dry. That's a concrete harm. Under YES, the state takes on $550M/yr in debt service — a modest, spread cost for a 55-year asset.

Also, one risk: Prop 1 combined with Prop 38 adds $1.1B/yr; and Prop 37 is self-repaying. So the aggregate burden is still ~0.5% of GF revenue.

Also there's a nuance: the "no new taxes" claim — debt service is paid from existing revenues, so no new taxes, but it crowds out other spending. Under deficits, that crowd-out matters. But the crowd-out is small (0.25%).

Let me quickly check SPUR's recommendation and one more critical analysis (maybe Reason Foundation or a Hoover/LAO economist take), then decide.

Bond
Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs
Authorizes $10 billion in general obligation bonds to fund production of affordable and supportive housing and $1.25 billion in mortgage revenue bonds to fund a homeownership program for veterans and military families.
SPUR's Recommendation
California’s housing affordability crisis continues to worsen, largely because of a supply shortage and inadequate funding to build more. Even with lower construction costs, affordable housing construction and preservation would still require significant, consistent government subsidies. Thousands of approved affordable housing projects have stalled because of a lack of financing.
General obligation bonds are needed periodically to replenish funding for the state’s main affordable housing finance programs. Prop. 1’s proposed bond funds pair with state and federal Low Income Housing Tax Credits to finance affordable housing developments. This measure is critical to expanding affordable housing opportunities for lower-income residents across California through new construction, preservation, and homebuyer assistance. Funds would be distributed through well-established state programs with a proven track record of success.
Vote YES
What Prop. 1 Would Do
According to the California Housing Partnership, Proposition 1 will help finance more than 40,000 shovel-ready affordable rental homes and help 20,000 California households attain homeownership. 1 The bond proceeds would replenish key long-standing state affordable housing financing programs and be allocated as follows:
$5.10 billion for the Multifamily Housing Program. At least 10% of units in each development receiving these funds must be affordable to extremely low-income households.
$1.25 billion in self-supporting revenue bonds for the CalVet Home Loan Program to help veterans and military families buy a home. These bonds are repaid entirely through mortgage payments and do not rely on taxpayer funding.
$1.15 billion for supportive housing administered through the Multifamily Housing Program. The program requires funding to create a reserve account to cover operating deficits for developments receiving funding.
$750 million for the Portfolio Reinvestment Program to rehabilitate and extend the long-term affordability of state-funded multifamily rental housing projects that are at risk of conversion to market-rate housing.
$600 million for the CalHOME Program for new construction of affordable ownership homes.
$500 million for the My Home down payment assistance program for lower- and moderate-income households.
$500 million for the Infill Infrastructure Grant Program of 2019 for grants supporting infrastructure needed to support developing affordable and mixed-income housing in infill locations.
$450 million to the Joe Serna, Jr. Farmworker Housing Program to fund grants or loans for the construction or rehabilitation of housing for agricultural employees and their families.
$350 million for new affordable student housing projects split evenly between the University of California and California State University systems.
$200 million for the Tribal Housing Grant Program to finance housing and housing-related activities enabling tribes to rebuild and reconstitute their communities.
$200 million for a program to be created by the Legislature that funds acquisition and rehabilitation of unrestricted housing units (i.e., unsubsidized housing that may naturally be affordable) and the attachment of long-term affordability restrictions to the units.
$200 million to the Local Housing Trust Fund Program to fund competitive grants and loans to local housing trust funds that develop, own, lend, or create or preserve affordable housing.
The Backstory
The state has historically used voter-approved general obligation bonds to fund affordable housing programs. In 2018, voters approved Proposition 1, the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2018, which provided $4 billion in funding, including $1 billion for the Department of Veterans Affairs program and $3 billion for various affordable housing programs. As of fiscal year 2023–24, when the 2018 Prop. 1 bond funding ran out, 22,735 units of housing had been produced.
Enterprise Community Partners’ 2026 California Affordable Housing Production Pipeline report, released in March, found that nearly 40,000 approved affordable housing units are frozen due to a lack of funding and could be built with this new financing source. 2
The proposed bond has undergone a rigorous process and has broad support. Over the past four years, the Legislature has introduced various affordable housing bond measures, including bills by Assemblymember Wicks and Senator Cabaldon. Those bills have moved through the legislative process over the past year and a half, giving the members of the Legislature multiple opportunities to negotiate the terms. Governor Newsom, Senate President Pro Tem Limón, and Assembly Speaker Rivas negotiated final amendments for the authorizing legislation, SB 417, the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026. The State Legislature voted with supermajorities in each house to place the proposition on the November 2026 ballot.
Legislative analyses of the measure find the total cost to pay off the bonds would be approximately $17.39 billion in principal and interest. Average annual debt service payments from the State’s General Fund are estimated at approximately $580 million when all bonds are sold, assuming an interest rate of 4.02% and a 30-year maturity. This amount of annual debt service represents about 0.26% of the State’s General Fund budget.
According to the State of California Debt Affordability Report issued by the state treasurer in October 2025, California’s ratio of General Fund-supported debt service to General Fund revenues was 3.59% in fiscal year 2024–25 and was estimated to be 3.95% in fiscal year 2025–26 . 3 This ratio is in line with the 4% historical average for bonded indebtedness.
A simple majority (50% plus one vote) of California voters is required to pass Prop. 1.
Equity Impacts
The Bay Area Equity Atlas finds that all nine Bay Area counties struggle to come anywhere close to meeting their state-mandated share of new housing construction. In 2023 and 2024, the Bay Area permitted just 9% of its required units, including only 5% of required very-low-income units and 10% of required low-income units. 4
This lack of affordable housing options increases displacement pressures on lower-income households and households of color. The Bay Area Equity Atlas’s Black Communities and the Bay Area's Housing Crisis report, published in April 2025, found the Bay Area lost more than 5,000 Black-owned households during the 2010s, with significant declines in historic Black communities in the East Bay, San Francisco, and Solano County, while the number of Black renter households increased by just 300. 5
Sufficient funding to create below-market-rate rental and homeownership opportunities will help address the affordability challenges and displacement pressures faced by lower-income households, Black households, and other households of color.
Pros
The state faces a chronic affordable housing crisis that cannot be addressed without significant ongoing public investment to lower housing costs for lower-income households.
The bond would make the most of recent federal changes to the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit program that allow California to nearly double its affordable housing production: if the state invests $4.1 billion annually, it can leverage $6.7 billion in available federal funding.
The funding would be distributed through existing state programs with a proven track record of producing affordable housing options for lower-income residents.
The Bay Area is well positioned to use the funds effectively, given the number of highly effective nonprofit affordable housing developers here.
Con
The bond would contribute to the state’s debt burden, with debt service on the bond representing 0.26% of the overall State General Fund budget.

Let me also check the CalMatters voter guide recommendation for Prop 1 (their editorial board recommended yes on Prop 1 based on the "answers yes to both questions" framing). Yes — the CalMatters commentary said Prop 1 "answers yes to both questions" (i.e., worth the investment).

Hmm, that's a bit higher than the LAO's 3% figure (different measurement: debt service vs GF revenue). The treasurer's ratio shows the state is at about the historical average, not below it. So capacity is roughly average — not a red flag, but not slack either. Adding Prop 1 + 38 pushes it above 4%.

Let me consider one more angle: are there cheaper alternatives to bonds? The state could fund housing from the General Fund, but the state is in structural deficit; it has already cut one-time housing investments. HJTA says "find $10 billion within general fund spending" — that's a hypothetical tradeoff (cutting other programs). Also note: interest rates on GO bonds vs. the state's alternative; some argue borrowing at ~4% while inflation is ~3% is cheap, and that capital assets should be debt-financed (intergenerational equity). The asset lasts 55+ years while the debt is repaid in 25-30 — standard public finance logic favors debt financing.

Overall, my judgment: YES.

Reasons:
1. Acute, well-documented need; ~40,000 permitted/shovel-ready affordable units stalled purely for lack of gap financing; state's key programs (MHP) exhausted and oversubscribed 9:1; prior bonds fully committed.
2. High leverage: each state dollar pulls in ~$4 of federal/local/private money; recent federal LIHTC changes amplify this; new state streamlining/CEQA/impact-fee reforms reduce per-unit costs, so this money goes further than earlier rounds.
3. Cost is small in context: $500-600M/yr ≈ 0.25% of the General Fund; 15% premium vs. cash is a normal, modest price for intergenerational equity on a 55-year asset; the $1.25B veterans portion is self-repaying at zero net cost.
4. Debt-service ratio ~3-4% of GF revenue is at/below historical norms; adding this bond (even with Prop 38) adds ~0.5%.
5. Broad, non-partisan coalition; no organized opposition, no rebuttal argument filed; legislature passed with supermajorities; endorsed by SF Chronicle, McClatchy boards, SPUR, CalMatters, LAist-neutral, Daily Bruin, etc.
6. The main "no" arguments — debt burden amid structural deficits and high per-unit costs — are real but modest in scale, and the deficits are driven by other spending; rejecting the bond doesn't solve them, while it would leave the housing pipeline stalled and the state's programs unfunded.

AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable housing, and downpayment assistance. YES

NO

PRO
Prop. 1 builds affordable homes for veterans, seniors, people with disabilities, low- and middle-income working families, vulnerable Californians and essential workers-teachers, firefighters and nurses. Requires strict fiscal accountability and public oversight with no new taxes.
CON

BACKGROUND
Public Sector Funds Some Home Building. In most years, about 100,000 houses and apartments are built in California. Most of these housing units are built entirely with private dollars. Some, however, receive financial help from federal, state, or local governments. In the case of housing funded by the state, the state government generally provides local governments, nonprofit organizations, and private developers with grants or low-cost loans to fund a portion of the housing units’ construction costs. Typically, housing built with these funds must be sold or rented to Californians with low incomes.
Bonds Are a Common Way for the State to Fund Home Building and Homeownership Programs. Over the past few decades, the state has used general obligation bonds to fund various housing programs. Bonds are a way the state borrows money to cover the up-front costs of a development and then repays the money plus interest over time. The last statewide general obligation bond for affordable housing was approved by voters in 2024, providing $2 billion to provide housing for veterans and other people with mental health or substance use challenges who are facing homelessness.
Home Loan Program for Veterans. The state’s veterans home loan program provides home loans to eligible veterans, including veterans who may not otherwise qualify for a home loan. Under the program, the state sells general obligation bonds to investors and uses the funds to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. Participating veterans repay the cost of the bonds through their payments on their home loan. The last statewide general obligation bond for veterans home loans was approved by voters in 2018, which provided $1 billion for the program.
PROPOSAL
New General Obligation Bond for Housing. Proposition 1 allows the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing purposes. This amount consists of (1) a $10 billion bond for a variety of state housing programs that would be repaid by the General Fund and (2) a $1.25 billion bond that would be repaid by veterans’ payments on their home loans. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons. For more information on the state’s General Fund-supported bonds, please see “Overview of State Bond Debt” later in this guide.)
State Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides bond funding for various types of housing programs, which are summarized in Figure 1. The funds would be allocated over a number of years. The major categories of housing programs supported by the bond are:
Affordable Multifamily Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $7.2 billion to acquire, build, or renovate rental housing, such as apartment buildings&#46 These programs generally provide local governments and private developers with low-interest loans to fund part of the project cost. In exchange, projects generally must reserve units for low-income households for a period of 55 years. Some of this funding would be used for supportive housing, which provides on-site service (such as mental health and substance use counseling) to certain residents.
Homeownership Programs. Proposition 1 provides $1.1 billion to support homeownership for low- and moderate-income households. Some of the funds would be used to provide homebuying assistance for first-time homebuyers through loans that generally do not have to be paid back until the home is sold or paid off. Other funds would be provided to nonprofit organizations and other entities for activities such as acquiring land to build homes for eligible low-income homebuyers and repairing existing homes owned by low-income households.
Infrastructure Programs. Proposition 1 provides $500 million for a variety of infrastructure projects to support affordable housing developments, such as water, sewage, parks, and transportation improvements.
Farmworker Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $450 million in loans and grants to build or renovate housing for farmworkers. Program funds could be used for both rental and owner-occupied housing.
Higher Education Student Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $350 million, split evenly between the University of California and California State University, for affordable student housing.
Tribal Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $200 million in grants to tribes. Funds could be used for various housing-related purposes, including construction and repair of rental and owner-occupied housing.
Local Pilot Programs. Proposition 1 provides $200 million that would be available to cities, counties, and certain other entities for pilot projects aimed at developing housing at reduced costs.
Veterans Housing Program. Proposition 1 also provides $1.25 billion for home loan assistance to veterans. Veterans generally use these loans to purchase single-family residences, condominiums, farms, and mobile homes.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost to Repay the $10 Billion Bond for Housing Programs. The state General Fund cost to repay the bond would be $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years . The estimated annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, the total cost of the bond would be about 15 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
No Direct State Cost for Veterans Housing Program. Veterans participating in the home loan program would make monthly payments to the state, allowing the state to repay the bonds. These payments have always covered the amount owed on the bonds, meaning the program has always operated at no direct cost to the state.
Administrative Costs. A number of state entities would experience increased costs to administer the various housing programs. A portion of the bond funds would cover these costs.
Impact of Funds. Much of the funding from Proposition 1 would be used together with other government monies to provide housing assistance. The bond funds would provide subsidies for up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, as well as about 2,500 units for farmworkers and about 1,200 beds for university students. The funds also would help up to 40,000 households, including about 2,100 veterans, with homeownership by providing homebuyer assistance and supporting the production and repair of homes.

Proposition 1: Housing Affordability
Proposition 1: Housing Affordability
Proposition 1: Authorizes Bonds For Housing Affordability Programs. Legislative Statute.
Additional Titles
Cali fornia Proposition 1, Veteran and Housing Assistance Programs Bond Measure
Summary
Proposition 1 is a legislatively referred bond measure which was passed by the California Legislature on June 26, 2026, through Senate Bill 417 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417) (SB 417). Both the Assembly and Senate votes exceeded the two-thirds majority required for the Legislature to place a bond measure before voters. Because legislatively referred bond measures also require the governor’s approval, Gov. Gavin Newsom’s signature on SB 417 completed the process of placing Proposition 1 on the ballot.
Proposition 1 would allow California to sell $11.25 billion through state bonds for housing programs. Of that amount, $10 billion would go toward housing assistance for low- and moderate-income Californians that would be repaid by the General Fund, while $1.25 billion would support the state’s home loan program for veterans.
The $10 billion for housing would fund a range of projects, including affordable rental housing, assistance for first-time homebuyers, farmworker and student housing, housing infrastructure, tribal housing projects, and local pilot programs aimed at lowering housing costs.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The state would repay the $10 billion housing portion from the General Fund, at an estimated cost of $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years. Veterans participating in the loan program would repay their home loans to the state. These payments are then used to pay back the bonds.
Because the state has to pay interest when it borrows money, the bond would cost about 15 percent more, after adjusting for inflation, than paying for the projects up front with money the state already has.
What your vote means (LAO's Analysis)
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could issue $11.25 billion in bonds to support housing programs for income-qualified Californians.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not issue the proposed $11.25 billion in bonds for low-income housing programs.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Proponents argue that California’s housing affordability and homelessness crises require substantial public investment and that Proposition 1 would directly improve the lives of people struggling to find or keep stable housing. They contend that funding affordable housing construction and preservation, homeownership assistance, and housing for veterans, farmworkers, students, and homeless and foster youth would provide meaningful help to Californians most affected by high housing costs.
Opponents argue that California should not take on additional debt for housing when the state has substantial revenues and could fund these programs directly. They contend that the underlying housing problem is a shortage of available homes caused largely by regulations and development restrictions, rather than a lack of government spending on affordable housing.

Photo by Damian Dovarganes, AP Photo In summary Supporters say California desperately needs money to fund housing construction and make a dent in its homelessness and affordability crisis. Critics say bond financing isn’t the way to do it. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) aims to address that crisis. It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/05/point-in-time-homelessness-report/) are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week (https://nlihc.org/oor/state/ca) to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/08/california-rhna-housing-affordable-progress/) of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes. Legislators have passed multiple laws (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/newsom-signs-massive-california-housing-overhaul/) trying to address that (https://calmatters.org/education/2026/10/new-laws-affordable-student-housing-california/) by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money. A recent report estimated (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/03/affordable-housing-bottleneck/) nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them. What would Prop. 1 do? If it passes, Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to fund various types of housing, including homes for veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. Where would the money go? Prop. 1 would fund a variety of programs. Here’s how it breaks down: $7.2 billion to buy, build or renovate apartment buildings, generally through low-interest loans to developers. Projects funded this way would have to reserve a certain number of units for low-income households. Some would be used for “supportive housing,” homeless housing that includes additional services. This, in combination with other funding sources, would help support up to 40,000 rental units, according to (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office. $1.25 billion to help veterans secure loans to buy homes. $1.1 billion to help low and moderate-income households buy homes. $500 million for the infrastructure that supports new housing construction, such as water, sewage, parks and transportation improvements. $450 million to build or renovate an estimated 2,500 units of farmworker housing. $350 million to fund affordable homes for an estimated 1,200 University of California and California State University students. $200 million in housing grants to tribes, which could fund both home construction and renovation. $200 million up for grabs to cities, counties and other groups that pitch pilot projects to develop low-cost housing. How would California pay for it? It would cost the state between $500 million and $600 million each year for about 25 years to repay the cost of the general housing bond, according to the legislative analyst. That money would come from the state’s general fund, and factors in interest. The $1.25 billion for veterans housing would not cost the state anything, as participating vets would pay it off through monthly loan payments. Have we done anything like this before? California voters approved (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2024/03/election-result-proposition-1/) (by the slimmest of margins) another bond (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/03/prop-1-update/) in 2024 that provided $2 billion to fund homes (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/) for people who need mental health and addiction services and veterans. That 2024 bond also was dubbed Prop. 1. What do supporters say? Supporters include housing developers and advocates, veterans groups, the California State University and University of California boards, groups representing California’s cities and counties, Democratic legislators and Gov. Gavin Newsom. Donors backing Prop. 1 also reflect some who would benefit. The campaign has received more than $12 million, including about $2 million from carpenters’ unions, $1 million from Airbnb and $1 million from Building a Better California, a PAC funded by Google founder Sergey Brin and other Silicon Valley billionaires. Sign up for free Δ Vivian Wan, chief executive of affordable housing provider Abode, says her organization has four projects with a planned total of about 230 units in the works that she hopes Prop. 1 will fund. Three are in the Bay Area and one is in Yolo County. Without that cash infusion, all four projects are stalled, she said. Projects for homeless and low-income residents need large subsidies since their tenants don’t pay enough in rent to offset the cost of building. They often also have to fund additional services, such as case managers to help residents navigate their physical and mental health, addictions, finances and more. City and county dollars can pay for some but not all of that. Prop. 1 would be “huge,” Wan said. But it wouldn’t magically solve the housing crisis. “Is it enough? Absolutely not,” she said. “We are lightyears behind in terms of production to meet the need. We have underinvested in housing for decades. This is going to help, for sure, but we really need a permanent source.” What do opponents say? When this measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) came up for a floor vote before the Legislature, two Republican senators voted no, as well as seven Republican assemblymembers. Sen. Tony Strickland (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/tony-strickland-188489), a Republican from Huntington Beach who opposed the bill, said calling it “The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026” amounted to a bait-and-switch maneuver, as only a small fraction of the total funds go to vets. “It really just says that you’re using veterans to pass your $10 billion general obligation bond,” he said during a June hearing. And, he said, there are better ways to get families into housing than using a bond to “borrow money against the future.” The strong revenues California experienced this year won’t continue, making it risky to push the state deeper into debt, he said. By Marisa Kendall, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 aims to address that crisis.

It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. 

A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes.

Legislators have passed multiple laws trying to address that by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money.

Also check the CBPC issue brief for the "each state dollar draws $4" claim, and the argument that the 2018 Prop 1 housing bond ($4 billion) has been fully committed/spent.

Let me also check the specific pro argument text (already have it) and the con side from the "californiachoices.org" page.
